title: How to look at an image — Image Wiki
text:
How to look at an image
  A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.

  
    Termformal analysis
    Also calledvisual analysis, reading an image
    Not the same astaste, interpretation, subject matter
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The one move that makes the rest workLook in this orderWhat this buys youA caution about rules
      
    
  

  Put two people in front of the same photograph. One says "yeah, it's nice." The other says "the light on her face comes from the left, but her shadow on the wall goes left too — so there are two suns."
The second person is not more talented. They have names for things, and a habit of looking in a fixed order. Both are learnable in an afternoon. Everything else in this wiki is the vocabulary; this page is the habit.
The one move that makes the rest work
Separate what the image shows from how it is put together.
The subject arrives free, in about 100 milliseconds, and you cannot stop noticing it. The construction has to be looked for — and it is where nearly all the quality lives. A photo of a beautiful place can be a bad image. A photo of a parking meter can be a good one.
The trick for forcing the switch is childishly simple: squint until the detail blurs out. What survives is the structure. What disappears was detail.


Rothstein's dust storm as photographed
The same file blurred by us, standing in for a squint


Arthur Rothstein, Dust storm, Cimarron County, Oklahoma, April 1936. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain. The right panel is our own blur of the left one.
Squinting, done arithmetically. Everything on the right collapses into four things: a pale sky, a mid-grey ground, one dark horizontal mass — the shed — and two small dark accents. Nothing else in the frame survives: the corrugated iron, the boards, the fence wire were detail sitting on a structure that works without them.
One thing the blur reveals that the sharp version hides. There are three people on the left panel, but only two dark accents on the right: the boy walking behind the man has merged into him. At squint size they are a single shape, and that is how the photograph actually reads.





Eugène Atget, Boucherie, Rue Christine, Paris, between 1895 and 1927. Library of Congress. Public domain.
The subject is a butcher's window. Nothing is beautiful and nothing is happening. Now describe the construction instead: one bright shape — the hanging meat and the marble sill — held inside a much darker frame of stone and shuttered wood, with the open doorway to its left as the deepest black in the picture. The only other light anywhere is the strip of pavement along the bottom edge, and it is kept flat and empty.
That is why a photograph of nothing holds together, and it is the whole argument against judging an image by what it is a picture of.


Look in this order
The order matters, because some observations are destroyed by the ones that come after.
1. Note where your eye landed first — before you think. You get exactly one shot at this per image. The instant you start analysing, you lose the ability to know where you actually looked. Whatever it was, that is the image's real focal point, regardless of what the maker intended. See Visual hierarchy.
2. Squint and find the big shapes. Three to five patches of light and dark, no more. Can you tell what the picture is from these alone? If the subject vanishes into the background at this stage, the image has a value problem, and no amount of colour or detail will fix it. See Value structure.



Dorothea Lange, Migrant Mother, Nipomo, California, 1936. Library of Congress, public domain.
Steps 1 and 2 on one frame. Where did you land? Her face — and squinting shows why. The tent, the clothes and the children all collapse into one mid-grey, and the only light shape left is her forehead, cheek and hand, which is also the only sharply detailed area in the picture. That is not luck: both older children have turned their faces into her shoulders, so there is no second face to compete, and the baby is a pale blur at the bottom edge.
Step 3 falls out of the same look. Her nose casts a small shadow straight down rather than across a cheek and the transitions across her face are gradual, so the light is soft, frontal and from above.


3. Find the light. Where is it coming from, and is it big and soft or small and hard? Then check whether every object in the frame agrees with that answer. Shadows are the evidence, so read the shadows, not the highlights. See Light direction and Hard and soft light.



Jack Delano, Chicago, Illinois. In the waiting room of Union Station, January 1943. Office of War Information, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Step 3 is usually detective work; here the evidence is lying in the open. The clerestory windows are in the top of the frame, and every beam leaves them heading down and to the right at the same angle — one source, high and to our left. Check that against the floor: the bright pools land to the lower right of the windows that made them, and where a body interrupts a beam the floor behind it stays dark.
Then do step 4 on the same picture. Your eye entered at the windows, slid down a beam and stopped on the two policemen — the darkest shapes standing in the brightest patch in the frame. The rays are not decoration, they are the path.


4. Trace where your eye goes next. Follow it for a few seconds. Does it move somewhere and settle, or bounce between two equally loud things, or slide out of the frame at a corner and not come back? An image that leaks at the edges feels restless and most people cannot say why.
5. Check the frame itself. What got cut off, and where? Is anything touching an edge awkwardly, or accidentally lined up — a pole rising out of a head, a horizon slicing through a neck? Your grouping machinery merges things that touch, and it does not care that the pole is thirty metres behind the head. See Gestalt grouping.
6. Only now, ask whether it works. By this point you should be able to say why, and the why should be a sentence about the image, not about your mood.

Describe, then interpret, then judge — in that order
Description is what is verifiably there: "the left half is in shadow." Interpretation is what it does: "the shadow hides his expression, so he reads as guarded." Judgement is whether it works: "that fits the scene, so yes." Most bad image criticism is judgement wearing a description's clothes — "the lighting is bad" is a verdict pretending to be an observation. Sliding from step one to step three without stopping at step two is the single most common failure, and it is why so many critiques are unusable to the person who made the thing.

What this buys you



Vague
Usable




"It looks flat."
"Everything is the same mid-value, so nothing separates from the background."


"Something's off."
"The face is lit from the left, the cast shadow says the light is on the right."


"It's too busy."
"Four things have equal contrast, so the eye never settles."


"It looks fake."
"The car has no contact shadow — it floats a few centimetres above the road."


"Bad composition."
"The subject is dead centre and cropped at the elbows, so it reads as a snapshot."



The right-hand column is not more sophisticated. It is the same perception, named. The naming is what makes it repeatable tomorrow, transferable to someone else, and defensible when a colleague disagrees.
A caution about rules
You will run into a lot of numbered rules — thirds, golden ratios, leading lines, triangles. Treat them as descriptions of things that often work, never as tests an image must pass. Plenty of excellent images break every one of them, and an image can satisfy all of them and still be dead. When a rule and your eye disagree, trust the eye and then work out what the eye is responding to. That is the whole skill.

The 30-second pass

Where did your eye go first? (Answer before you think.)
Squint: what are the three biggest light and dark shapes?
Where is the light, and does every shadow agree?
Where does the eye go second, and does it settle?
Anything merging, colliding, or cut off at an edge?
Now say what works and what does not — in a sentence about the image.
